# Computation of small reflective and dihedral Ramsey numbers

**Abstract**

Throughout, all graphs are simple, finite and have vertex sets of the form {0,1,2_,...,n_-1} for some \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). For graphs _G_ and _H_, and a permutation group \(\Gamma\) on the vertex set of _H_, we say that _H_ is \(\Gamma\)_-embeddable_ in _G_ if there exists a graph homomorphism from _H_ to _G_ of the form \(\psi\circ\varphi\), where \(\varphi\in\Gamma\) and \(\psi\) is an increasing injection. Recently, standard and ordered Ramsey numbers of graphs were unified through the introduction of permutational Ramsey numbers, defined as follows. For graphs _H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_ and permutation groups \(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\dots,\Gamma_k\) on their respective vertex sets, the _permutational Ramsey number_ \(R(H_1^{\Gamma_1},H_2^{\Gamma_2},\dots,H_k^{\Gamma_k})\) is the minimum \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) such that for every _k_-edge-coloring of a complete graph on _n_ vertices, there exists some \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\) for which _H<sub>j</sub>_ is \(\Gamma_j\)-embeddable in the spanning subgraph of the complete graph comprising the edges of color _j_.

Here, we consider reflective (resp. dihedral) Ramsey numbers, which are a specific class of permutational Ramsey numbers in which each group \(\Gamma_j\) is the reflection group (resp. dihedral group) on the naturally ordered vertex set of _H<sub>j</sub>_. Focusing on the two-color case, we apply the SAT-based approach originally proposed by Poljak for ordered Ramsey numbers and recently extended to cyclic Ramsey numbers. We utilize the Kissat SAT solver to obtain exact values and lower bounds for small reflective and dihedral Ramsey numbers whose two arguments belong to the following graph classes: monotone and alternating paths, monotone cycles, start-central stars, complete graphs and nested matchings. We also derive several general results and formulate conjectures based on the computational findings.

**Keywords:** Ramsey numbers, reflective Ramsey numbers, dihedral Ramsey numbers, permutational Ramsey numbers, SAT.

**Mathematics Subject Classification (2020):** 05D10, 05C55.

### 1 Introduction

We consider all graphs to be undirected, simple and finite, with vertex sets of the form {0,1,2_,...,n_-1} for some \(n\in\mathbb{N}\). For a graph _G_, we denote its vertex and edge sets by _V(G_) and _E(G_), respectively, and write |_G_| for its order. We write _K<sub>n</sub>_ for the complete graph on _n_ vertices. A _k_-edge-coloring of a graph _G_ is a mapping from _E(G_) to {1,2_,...,k_}.

Ramsey theory originates from a theorem of Ramsey [25], which asserts that for any graphs _H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_, every _k_-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_ contains a monochromatic copy of _H<sub>j</sub>_ in color _j_, for some \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\), provided that \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) is sufficiently large. The minimum such _n_ is called the _Ramsey number R(H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_). Although the definition of Ramsey numbers is straightforward, determining their exact values is often remarkably difficult. Indeed, even the diagonal Ramsey number _R(K_<sub>5</sub>_,K_<sub>5</sub>) remains unknown [24]. Ramsey-type phenomena have been investigated in numerous settings over the past century, leading to a rich literature on a variety of combinatorial structures, including hypergraphs, ordered graphs, geometric configurations, and sequences; see [11,13-15,17,20-22,24] and the references therein.

Among the many directions in modern Ramsey theory, ordered Ramsey numbers have received considerable attention in recent years. Given graphs _H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_, the _ordered Ramsey number_ Rord(_H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_) is defined as the minimum \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) such that for every _k_-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_, there exists an increasing injective homomorphism from _H<sub>j</sub>_ to the spanning subgraph of _K<sub>n</sub>_ comprising the edges of color _j_, for some \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\). The systematic study of ordered Ramsey numbers was initiated independently by Balko, Cibulka, Král and Kynčl [2,3], and Conlon, Fox, Lee and Sudakov [10]. For a selection of recent results on the asymptotic properties of ordered Ramsey numbers, see the survey [1] by Balko and the references therein.

Recently, standard and ordered Ramsey numbers were unified within a group-theoretic framework through the introduction of permutational Ramsey numbers \[4\]. For convenience, we first introduce the following terminology. Let _G_ and _H_ be graphs, and let \(\Gamma\) be a permutation group on _V(H_). We say that _H_ is \(\Gamma\)_-embeddable_ in _G_ if there exists a graph homomorphism from _H_ to _G_ of the form \(\psi\circ\varphi\), where \(\varphi\in\Gamma\) and \(\psi:V(H)\rightarrow V(G)\) is an increasing injection. Using this terminology, the definition of permutational Ramsey numbers from \[4\] can be stated as follows. For graphs _H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_ and permutation groups \(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\dots,\Gamma_k\) on their respective vertex sets, the _permutational Ramsey number_ \(R(H_1^{\Gamma_1},H_2^{\Gamma_2},\dots,H_k^{\Gamma_k})\) is the minimum \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) such that for every _k_-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_, there exists some \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\) for which _H<sub>j</sub>_ is \(\Gamma_j\)-embeddable in the spanning subgraph of _K<sub>n</sub>_ comprising the edges of color _j_. The well-definedness of permutational Ramsey numbers follows directly from Ramsey’s theorem \[25\].

Different choices of permutation groups give rise to several previously studied classes of Ramsey numbers. In particular, standard Ramsey numbers are obtained by taking each \(\Gamma_j\) to be the symmetric group on _V(H<sub>j</sub>_), whereas ordered Ramsey numbers are obtained by taking each \(\Gamma_j\) to be the trivial permutation group on _V(H<sub>j</sub>_). The same framework also encompasses cyclic Ramsey numbers _R_<sub>cyc</sub>(_H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_), introduced and investigated in \[4\], which arise by taking each \(\Gamma_j\) to be the cyclic group generated by the cyclic shift permutation with respect to the natural vertex order, i.e., \(\Gamma_j=\left\langle\left(\begin{array}{ c c c }
0 & 1 & 2 & \cdots \\
1 & 2 & 3 & \cdots \\
H_j|-1 & 0 & 
\end{array}\right)\right\rangle\) for each \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\).

Motivated by the results of \[4\] on the computation of small ordered and cyclic Ramsey numbers, we investigate two other natural classes of permutational Ramsey numbers proposed in the same paper:

**(1)** the reflective Ramsey numbers _R_<sub>ref</sub>(_H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_), which arise by taking each \(\Gamma_j\) to be the group gener ated by the reflection with respect to the natural vertex order, i.e., \(\Gamma_j=\left\langle\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c }
0 & 1 & 2 & \cdots \\
|H_j|-1 & |H_j|-2 & |H_j|-3 & \cdots \\
|H_j|-1 & |H_j|-2 & |H_j|-3 & 0
\end{array}\right)\right\rangle\) for each \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\); and

**(2)** the dihedral Ramsey numbers _R_<sub>dih</sub>(_H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_), which arise by taking each \(\Gamma_j\) to be the group generated by the cyclic shift permutation and the reflection with respect to the natural vertex order, i.e.,

\(\Gamma_j=\left\langle\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c }
0 & 1 & 2 & \cdots \\
1 & 2 & 3 & \cdots \\
|H_j|-1 & 0 & 
\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c }
0 & 1 & 2 & \cdots \\
|H_j|-1 & |H_j|-1 & |H_j|-3 & \cdots \\
|H_j|-1 & |H_j|-2 & |H_j|-3 & 0
\end{array}\right)\right\rangle\)

for each \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\).

It is natural to study reflective (resp. dihedral) Ramsey numbers because they correspond to graphs whose vertices are linearly (resp. cyclically) ordered, but the direction of the ordering is ignored, unlike in the ordered (resp. cyclic) Ramsey numbers.

We focus on the two-color case, with the goal of computing small reflective and dihedral Ramsey numbers whose arguments belong to the following graph classes: monotone and alternating paths, monotone cycles, start-central stars, complete graphs and nested matchings. Formal definitions of these graph classes are given in Section 2. The Ramsey numbers are computed by formulating Boolean satisfiability (SAT) problems that encode the search for a 2-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_ containing no forbidden embeddings, following the approach originally proposed by Poljak \[23\] for ordered Ramsey numbers and later extended to cyclic Ramsey numbers \[4\]. Due to its strong performance in the main track of the SAT Competition 2024, we use the Kissat SAT solver \[6, 7\] to handle all the resulting SAT instances. We automate the computation of small reflective and dihedral Ramsey numbers by using and extending the source code available at \[5\], originally developed for computing ordered and cyclic Ramsey numbers. We also establish several general results and formulate conjectures motivated by the computational findings.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the necessary terminology, establishes some basic properties of permutational Ramsey numbers and formally defines the graph classes considered throughout the paper. Section 3 describes the SAT-based approach and the software used to compute small reflective and dihedral Ramsey numbers. Section 4 presents the computational results, establishes several general results, formulates conjectures motivated by the computational findings and compares the computed Ramsey numbers with the previously known ordered and cyclic Ramsey numbers. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper with a brief summary and directions for future research. The source code used to obtain the computational results is available at \[12\], together with supplementary data, including the computed Ramsey numbers, the Kissat output files and all the 2-edge-colorings yielding the lower bounds.

## 2 Preliminaries

We begin with the following notion, originally introduced in \[4\]. Let _G_<sub>1</sub> and _G_<sub>2</sub> be graphs of the same order, and let \(\Gamma\) be a permutation group on _V(G_<sub>1</sub>)=_V(G_<sub>2</sub>). We say that _G_<sub>1</sub> is \(\Gamma\)_-isomorphic_ to _G_<sub>2</sub>, and write \(G_1\cong_\Gamma G_2\), if there exists an isomorphism \(\varphi\) from _G_<sub>1</sub> to _G_<sub>2</sub> such that \(\varphi\in\Gamma\). The relation \(\cong_\Gamma\) is clearly an equivalence relation. Moreover, graphs belonging to the same equivalence class are interchangeable as arguments of a permutational Ramsey number whenever the associated permutation group is \(\Gamma\).

**Proposition 2.1.** _Let H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub> be graphs and let_ \(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\dots,\Gamma_k\) _be permutation groups on their respective vertex sets. Suppose that F_<sub>1</sub>_,F_<sub>2</sub>_,...,F<sub>k</sub> are graphs such that_ \(F_j\cong_{\Gamma_j}H_j\) _for each_ \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\)_. Then_ \(R(F_1^{\Gamma_1},F_2^{\Gamma_2},\dots,F_k^{\Gamma_k})=R(H_1^{\Gamma_1},H_2^{\Gamma_2},\dots,H_k^{\Gamma_k})\).

_Proof._ Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and consider a _k_-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_. For each \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\), let _G<sub>j</sub>_ denote the spanning subgraph of _K<sub>n</sub>_ comprising the edges of color _j_. Suppose that there exists \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\) such that _H<sub>j</sub>_ is \(\Gamma_j\)-embeddable in _G<sub>j</sub>_. By symmetry, it suffices to show that _F<sub>j</sub>_ is also \(\Gamma_j\)-embeddable in _G<sub>j</sub>_. By the definition of \(\Gamma_j\)-embeddability, there exists a homomorphism from _H<sub>j</sub>_ to _G<sub>j</sub>_ of the form \(\psi\circ\varphi\), where \(\varphi\in\Gamma_j\) and \(\psi:V(H_j)\rightarrow V(G_j)\) is an increasing injection. Since \(F_j\cong_{\Gamma_j}H_j\), there exists an isomorphism \(\chi\in\Gamma_j\) from _F<sub>j</sub>_ to _H<sub>j</sub>_. Therefore, \(\psi\circ(\varphi\circ\chi)\) is a homomorphism from _F<sub>j</sub>_ to _G<sub>j</sub>_, with \(\varphi\circ\chi\in\Gamma_j\) and \(\psi\) an increasing injection. Hence, _F<sub>j</sub>_ is \(\Gamma_j\)-embeddable in _G<sub>j</sub>_.

Complementing Proposition 2.1, which treats changes of the arguments, we now consider changes in the associated permutation groups. The following observation establishes a monotonicity property with respect to these groups.

**Proposition 2.2.** _Let H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub> be graphs, and let_ \(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\dots,\Gamma_k\) _and_ \(\Lambda_1,\Lambda_2,\dots,\Lambda_k\) _be permutation groups on their respective vertex sets. Suppose that_ \(\Gamma_j\le\Lambda_j\) _for each_ \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\)_. Then_ \(R(H_1^{\Lambda_1},H_2^{\Lambda_2},\dots,H_k^{\Lambda_k})\le R(H_1^{\Gamma_1},H_2^{\Gamma_2},\dots,H_k^{\Gamma_k})\).

**Corollary 2.3.** _Let H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub> be graphs and let_ \(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\dots,\Gamma_k\) _be permutation groups on their respective vertex sets. Then_ \(R(H_1,H_2,\dots,H_k)\le R(H_1^{\Gamma_1},H_2^{\Gamma_2},\dots,H_k^{\Gamma_k})\le R_\mathrm{ord}(H_1,H_2,\dots,H_k)\).

Given graphs _G_ and _H_, and a permutation group \(\Gamma\) on _V(H_), it is straightforward to observe that the following two statements are equivalent.

**(1)** _H_ is \(\Gamma\)-embeddable in _G_.

**(2)** There exists a graph \(F\cong_\Gamma H\) with an increasing injective homomorphism from _F_ to _G_.

This yields the following result.

**Proposition 2.4.** _Let H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub> be graphs, and let_ \(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\dots,\Gamma_k\) _and_ \(\Lambda_1,\Lambda_2,\dots,\Lambda_k\) _be permutation groups on their respective vertex sets. Suppose that, for each_ \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\)_, H<sub>j</sub> lies in the same equivalence class under both_ \(\cong_{\Gamma_j}\) _and_ \(\cong_{\Lambda_j}\)_. Then_ \(R(H_1^{\Lambda_1},H_2^{\Lambda_2},\dots,H_k^{\Lambda_k})=R(H_1^{\Gamma_1},H_2^{\Gamma_2},\dots,H_k^{\Gamma_k})\).

A graph _H_ is said to have _reflection symmetry_ if the mapping \(\varphi:V(H)\rightarrow V(H)\) defined by \(\varphi(x)=|H|-1-x\) is an automorphism of _H_. The following corollary of Proposition 2.4 is immediate for graphs with reflection symmetry.

**Corollary 2.5.** _For any graphs H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub> with reflection symmetry, we have R_<sub>ref</sub>(_H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_)=_R_<sub>ord</sub>(_H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_) _and R_<sub>dih</sub>(_H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_)=_R_<sub>cyc</sub>(_H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>)._

The following corollary is another consequence of Proposition 2.4.

**Corollary 2.6.** _Let H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub> be graphs such that each graph is a start-central star or has reflection symmetry. Then_ \(R_\mathrm{dih}(H_1,H_2,\dots,H_k)=R_\mathrm{cyc}(H_1,H_2,\dots,H_k)\).

Now, we formally define each of the graph classes relevant to our work. For any \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), the _monotone path_ \(P_n^\mathrm{mon}\) is the graph of order _n_ in which any two vertices are adjacent if and only if they are consecutive integers, while the _alternating path_ \(P_n^\mathrm{alt}\) is the path graph of order _n_ with the underlying path \((0,n-1,1,n-2,2,n-3,\dots,\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)\); see Figure 1. For any \(n\ge 3\), the _monotone cycle_ \(C_n^\mathrm{mon}\) is the graph obtained from \(P_n^\mathrm{mon}\) by adding the edge {0_,n_-1}. Also, for convenience, we let \(C_2^\mathrm{mon}:=K_2\). Furthermore, for any \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), the _start-central star_ \(S_n^\mathrm{sc}\) is the star graph of order _n_ in which vertex 0 is adjacent to all the other vertices. Finally, for any even \(n\ge 2\), the _nested matching_ \(M_n^\mathrm{nest}\) is the 1-regular graph of order _n_ in which each vertex _v_ is adjacent only to _n_-1-_v_; see Figure 2.

The choice of graph classes of interest is motivated by the computational results of \[4\]. The same graph classes are considered, with the exception of reverse alternating paths, which arise by reflecting alternating paths and are therefore equivalent to them in the context of reflective and dihedral Ramsey numbers. Furthermore, by Corollaries 2.5 and 2.6, it suffices to consider reflective Ramsey numbers in which at least one argument lacks reflection symmetry, and dihedral Ramsey numbers in which at least one argument is an alternating path. Otherwise, the problem reduces to computing an ordered or a cyclic Ramsey number, respectively, which was already investigated in \[4\]. Thus, we are interested in computing the reflective Ramsey numbers of alternating paths and start-central stars versus all the considered graph classes, together with the dihedral Ramsey numbers of alternating paths versus all the considered graph classes.

We conclude this section with the following lemma.

**Lemma 2.7.** _Let H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub> and F be graphs such that there exists an increasing injective homomorphism from F to H_<sub>1</sub>_. Then_ \(R_\text{type}(F,H_2,\dots,H_k)\unknown R_\text{type}(H_1,H_2,\dots,H_k)\) _for each_ \(\text{type}\in\{\text{ord},\text{ref},\text{cyc},\text{dih}\}\).

_Proof._ Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and consider a _k_-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_. Let _G_ denote the spanning subgraph of _K<sub>n</sub>_ comprising the edges of color 1. Furthermore, let \(\Gamma\) and \(\Lambda\) denote the permutation groups associated with _H_<sub>1</sub> and _F_, respectively, in the permutational Ramsey numbers _R_type(_H_<sub>1</sub>_,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_) and _R_type(_F,H_<sub>2</sub>_,...,H<sub>k</sub>_). To complete the proof, it suffices to show that if _H_<sub>1</sub> is \(\Gamma\)-embeddable in _G_, then _F_ is \(\Lambda\)-embeddable in _G_.

Let \(\chi\) be an increasing injective homomorphism from _F_ to _H_<sub>1</sub>, and suppose that there exists a homomorphism from _H_<sub>1</sub> to _G_ of the form \(\psi_1\circ\varphi_1\), where \(\varphi_1\in\Gamma\) and \(\psi_1:V(H_1)\rightarrow V(G)\) is an increasing injection. Then \(f:=\psi_1\circ\varphi_1\circ\chi\) is an injective homomorphism from _F_ to _G_. We carry out the proof by showing that _f_ can be written as \(f=\psi_2\circ\varphi_2\) for some \(\varphi_2\in\Lambda\) and increasing injection \(\psi_2:V(F)\rightarrow V(G)\).

If type=ord, then \(\varphi_1\) is the identity permutation, so _f_ is increasing, which directly gives the desired result. On the other hand, if type=ref, then \(\varphi_1\) is either the identity permutation, in which case we are done, or \(\varphi_1\) is the reflection with respect to the natural vertex order. In the latter case, we have \(\varphi_1(x)=|H_1|-1-x\) for each \(x\in V(H_1)\), which implies that _f_ is decreasing. By defining \(\varphi_2\in\Lambda\) via \(\varphi_2(x)=|F|-1-x\) for each \(x\in V(F)\), it follows that \(\psi_2:=f\circ\varphi_2\) is an increasing injection from _V(F_) to _V(G_). Therefore, \(f=\psi_2\circ\varphi_2^{-1}=\psi_2\circ\varphi_2\) is the desired representation of _f_.

Next, suppose that type=cyc. Here, we have \(\varphi_1=g^p\) for \(g=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c }
0 & 1 & 2 & \cdots & |H_1|-2 & |H_1|-1 \\
1 & 2 & 3 & \cdots & |H_1|-1 & 0
\end{array}\right)\) and some \(p\in\mathbb{N}\). First, we show that for any increasing injection \(h_1:V(F)\rightarrow V(H_1)\), the map \(g\circ h_1\) can be written as \(g\circ h_1=h_2\circ r\) for some \(r\in\Lambda\) and increasing injection \(h_2:V(F)\rightarrow V(H_1)\). If \(h_1(|F|-1)\neq|H_1|-1\), then \(g\circ h_1\) is increasing, so we are done. Otherwise, \((g\circ h_1)(|F|-1)=0\) and \(1\unknown(g\circ h_1)(0)\unknown(g\circ h_1)(1)\unknown\cdots\unknown(g\circ h_1)(|F|-2)\). By letting \(r:=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c }
0 & 1 & 2 & \cdots & |F|-2 & |F|-1 \\
1 & 2 & 3 & \cdots & |F|-1 & 0
\end{array}\right)\), it follows that \(h_2:=(g\circ h_1)\circ r^{-1}\) is an increasing injection, so \(g\circ h_1=h_2\circ r\) is the desired representation of \(g\circ h_1\). Now, by a simple induction on _p_, we conclude that for any increasing injection \(h_1:V(F)\rightarrow V(H_1)\), the map \(g^p\circ h_1\) can also be written as \(g^p\circ h_1=h_2\circ r\) for some \(r\in\Lambda\) and increasing injection \(h_2:V(F)\rightarrow V(H_1)\). By applying this observation to \(g^p\circ\chi\), we obtain \(f=\psi_1\circ g^p\circ\chi=\psi_1\circ h_2\circ r\), so the original desired representation follows by letting \(\psi_2:=\psi_1\circ h_2\) and \(\varphi_2:=r\).

Finally, suppose that type=dih, and let _g_ be defined as above. In this situation, either \(\varphi_1=g^p\) for some \(p\in\mathbb{N}\), or \(\varphi_1=t\circ g^p\) for \(t=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c }
0 & 1 & 2 & \cdots & |H_1|-1 \\
|H_1|-1 & |H_1|-2 & |H_1|-3 & \cdots & 0
\end{array}\right)\) and some \(p\in\mathbb{N}\). In the former case, the result is proved in the same manner as in the case type=cyc. In the latter case, we have \(f=\psi_1\circ t\circ g^p\circ\chi\), so by the results from the case type=cyc, we conclude that _f_ can be written as \(f=\psi_1\circ t\circ h_2\circ r\), where _r=z<sup>q</sup>_ for \(z=\left(\begin{array}{ c c c c }
0 & 1 & 2 & \cdots & |F|-2 & |F|-1 \\
1 & 2 & 3 & \cdots & |F|-1 & 0
\end{array}\right)\) and some \(q\in\mathbb{N}\), and \(h_2:V(F)\rightarrow V(H_1)\) is an increasing injection. Now, define \(w\in\Lambda\) via _w(x_)=|_F_|-1-_x_ for each \(x\in V(F)\), and observe that \(\psi_2:=\psi_1\circ t\circ h_2\circ w\) is an increasing injection from _F_ to _G_. Therefore, \(\psi_1\circ t\circ h_2=\psi_2\circ w^{-1}=\psi_2\circ w\), which yields \(f=\psi_2\circ w\circ r\). The desired representation now follows by letting \(\varphi_2:=w\circ r\).

Our software for computing small reflective and dihedral Ramsey numbers relies on the following corollaries of Lemma 2.7.

**Corollary 2.8.** _Let H be any graph,_ \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) _and_ \(\text{type}\in\{\text{ord},\text{ref},\text{cyc},\text{dih}\}\)_. Then:_

**_(1)_** \(R_\text{type}(P_n^\text{mon},H)\le R_\text{type}(P_{n+1}^\text{mon},H)\);

**_(2)_** \(R_\text{type}(S_n^\text{sc},H)\le R_\text{type}(S_{n+1}^\text{sc},H)\)_; and_

**_(3)_** \(R_\text{type}(K_n,H)\le R_\text{type}(K_{n+1},H)\).

_Proof._ The result follows from Lemma 2.7 by observing that there exists an increasing injective homomorphism from \(P_n^\text{mon}\), \(S_n^\text{sc}\) and _K<sub>n</sub>_, to \(P_{n+1}^\text{mon}\), \(S_{n+1}^\text{sc}\) and _K_<sub>_n_+1</sub>, respectively.

**Corollary 2.9.** _Let H be any graph,_ \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) _be even and_ \(\text{type}\in\{\text{ord},\text{ref},\text{cyc},\text{dih}\}\)_. Then_ \(R_\text{type}(M_n^\text{nest},H)\le R_\text{type}(M_{n+2}^\text{nest},H)\).

_Proof._ The result follows from Lemma 2.7 by observing that there exists an increasing injective homomorphism from \(M_n^\text{nest}\) to \(M_{n+2}^\text{nest}\).

**Corollary 2.10.** _Let H be any graph,_ \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) _and_ \(\text{type}\in\{\text{ref},\text{dih}\}\)_. Then_ \(R_\text{type}(P_n^\text{alt},H)\le R_\text{type}(P_{n+1}^\text{alt},H)\).

_Proof._ Let \(P_{n+1}^\text{ralt}\) denote the reverse alternating path of order _n_+1, which arises by reflecting \(P_{n+1}^\text{alt}\) with respect to the natural vertex order. Then there exists an increasing injective homomorphism from \(P_n^\text{alt}\) to \(P_{n+1}^\text{ralt}\), so Lemma 2.7 gives \(R_\text{type}(P_n^\text{alt},H)\le R_\text{type}(P_{n+1}^\text{ralt},H)\). Since \(P_{n+1}^\text{ralt}\) and \(P_{n+1}^\text{alt}\) are equivalent in the context of reflective and dihedral Ramsey numbers, Proposition 2.1 gives \(R_\text{type}(P_{n+1}^\text{ralt},H)=R_\text{type}(P_{n+1}^\text{alt},H)\).

## 3 Methodology

In the present section, we describe how the computation of permutational Ramsey numbers can be carried out by solving SAT problems. Our approach is a direct generalization of the SAT-based approach originally proposed by Poljak for ordered Ramsey numbers \[23\] and recently extended to cyclic Ramsey numbers \[4\].

Let _H_<sub>1</sub> and _H_<sub>2</sub> be two graphs, and let \(\Gamma_1\) and \(\Gamma_2\) be two permutation groups on their respective vertex sets. Now, consider a 2-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_ for some \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), and let _G<sub>j</sub>_ be the spanning subgraph of _K<sub>n</sub>_ comprising the edges of color _j_, for \(j\in\{1,2\}\). For each \(\{u,v\}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(K_n)}{2}\), let _x_<sub>{_u,v_}</sub> be a Boolean variable indicating whether the edge {_u,v_} is colored with color 2. Also, let Inc(_V(H_<sub>1</sub>)_,V(K<sub>n</sub>_)) and Inc(_V(H_<sub>2</sub>)_,V(K<sub>n</sub>_)) denote the sets of all increasing injections from _V(H_<sub>1</sub>) to _V(K<sub>n</sub>_) and from _V(H_<sub>2</sub>) to _V(K<sub>n</sub>_), respectively.

In the context of computing the permutational Ramsey number \(R(H_1^{\Gamma_1},H_2^{\Gamma_2})\), the search for a 2-edge- coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_ containing no forbidden embeddings can be encoded as a SAT problem by observing that _H_<sub>1</sub> is not \(\Gamma_1\)-embeddable in _G_<sub>1</sub> if and only if<tbc>

\(\wedge_{\psi\in\text{Inc}(V(H_1),V(K_n))}\wedge_{\varphi\in\Gamma_1}\vee_{\{u,v\}\in E(H_1)}x_{\{(\psi\circ\varphi)(u),(\psi\circ\varphi)(v)\}},\) (1)

<tbc>while _H_<sub>2</sub> is not \(\Gamma_2\)-embeddable in _G_<sub>2</sub> if and only if

\(\wedge_{\psi\in\text{Inc}(V(H_2),V(K_n))}\wedge_{\varphi\in\Gamma_2}\vee_{\{u,v\}\in E(H_2)}\neg x_{\{(\psi\circ\varphi)(u),(\psi\circ\varphi)(v)\}}.\) (2)

Therefore, by combining (1) and (2), we obtain a SAT problem with \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}\) variables and \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{|H_1|}|\Gamma_1|+\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{|H_2|}|\Gamma_2|\) clauses. If the SAT problem is satisfiable, then there exists a 2-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_ containing no forbidden embeddings, hence \(R(H_1^{\Gamma_1},H_2^{\Gamma_2})\ge n+1\). Otherwise, such a 2-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_ does not exist, implying that \(R(H_1^{\Gamma_1},H_2^{\Gamma_2})\le n\). Therefore, solving the formulated SAT problem gives either a lower bound or an upper bound on \(R(H_1^{\Gamma_1},H_2^{\Gamma_2})\). The permutational Ramsey number can then be exactly computed by solving SAT instances for sufficiently many values of _n_.

Our computation of small reflective and dihedral Ramsey numbers of interest is automated through a pipeline of four `Python` modules:

**(1) sat\_problem\_generator.py;**

**(2) instance\_solver.py;**

**(3) number\_finder.py;** and

**(4) grid\_explorer.py.**<tbc>

The first module, `sat\_problem\_generator.py`, is essentially the `src/sat\_solving/cnf\_generator.py` script from \[5\], with small modifications made to provide a suitable API for the other modules. The other three modules are implemented from scratch and their core logic is based on the `bash` scripts in the `src/sat\_solving` folder from \[5\]. Our full source code is available at \[12\], together with supplementary data, including the computed Ramsey numbers, the Kissat output files and all the 2-edge-colorings yielding the lower bounds.

The `sat\_problem\_generator.py` script accepts two graphs _H_<sub>1</sub> and _H_<sub>2</sub> from the graph classes of interest, together with \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and a string indicating which type of Ramsey number is being considered. It then generates the corresponding SAT problem encoding the search for a 2-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_ containing no forbidden embeddings. The generated SAT instance is printed out in the standard DIMACS CNF format, with the Boolean variables _x_<sub>{_u,v_}</sub> arranged in ascending order first by min{_u,v_}, and then by max{_u,v_}, i.e., as

\(x_{\{0,1\}},x_{\{0,2\}},\dots,x_{\{0,n-1\}},x_{\{1,2\}},x_{\{1,3\}},\dots,x_{\{1,n-1\}},x_{\{2,3\}},x_{\{2,4\}},\dots,x_{\{2,n-1\}},\dots,x_{\{n-2,n-1\}}.\)

The script is executed with six required arguments using the following syntax:

`python sat\_problem\_generator.py \<class\_a\> \<a\> \<class\_b\> \<b\> \<problem\_type\> \<n\>`

Here, `class\_a` and `class\_b` are strings from the set {pmon, palt, cmon, ssc, k, mnest} that specify the graph classes of _H_<sub>1</sub> and _H_<sub>2</sub>, respectively, while `a` and `b` determine |_H_<sub>1</sub>| and |_H_<sub>2</sub>|. Furthermore, `problem\_type` is a string from the set {ord, ref, cyc, dih} indicating which of the four supported types of Ramsey numbers (ordered, reflective, cyclic and dihedral) is being considered, while `n` represents _n_.

**Example 3.1.** Consider the following command:

`python sat\_problem\_generator.py palt 4 pmon 5 ref 12`

This command prints out the DIMACS CNF representation of the SAT instance that encodes the search for a 2-edge-coloring of _K_<sub>12</sub> containing no forbidden embeddings in the context of the reflective Ramsey number \(R_\mathrm{ref}(P_4^\mathrm{alt},P_5^\mathrm{mon})\). \(\unknown\)

The `instance\_solver.py` module solves a SAT instance encoding the search for a 2-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_ containing no forbidden embeddings. It accepts the same arguments as the `sat\_problem\_generator.py` script, which is immediately invoked to generate an output DIMACS CNF file representing the generated SAT problem. Afterwards, the Kissat SAT solver is used on the output file in order to solve the generated SAT instance. Both of these steps have a time limit, and the execution is aborted in case of a timeout. Additionally, if the Kissat executable is not present, an auxiliary `bash` script from \[5\] is used to obtain it automatically. To avoid trivial cases where the Ramsey number is identically one, both argument graphs are required to have at least two vertices.

The main function of the `instance\_solver.py` module returns an ordered pair `(status, graph)`, as follows.

**(1)** If a timeout is reached, then both `status` and `graph` are set to `None`. In this case, it is not known whether the SAT instance has a solution.

**(2)** If the SAT instance is deemed unsatisfiable, then `status` is set to `False`, while `graph` is set to `None`.

**(3)** If the SAT instance is deemed satisfiable, then `status` is set to `True`, while `graph` is set to the `graph6` \[18, 19\] string representation of the solution found to the SAT instance. Here, the presence of an edge indicates that its color in _K<sub>n</sub>_ is 2, i.e., that the corresponding Boolean variable is `True`.

In addition, the `instance\_solver.py` module saves the Kissat outputs to separate files in the `kissat\_output` folder and, in the case of satisfiable instances, saves the `graph6` string representations of the corresponding solutions to separate files in the `parsed\_graphs` folder.

**Example 3.2.** Consider the following command:

`python instance\_solver.py palt 4 pmon 5 ref 12`

This command gives the following output:

`(True, ’KCrffr{^f}^{’)`

Therefore, the corresponding SAT instance is satisfiable, with the solution given as a `graph6` string. Hence, \(R_\mathrm{ref}(P_4^\mathrm{alt},P_5^\mathrm{mon})\unknown 13\). Now, consider the following command:

`python instance\_solver.py palt 4 pmon 5 ref 13`

Its execution gives the following output:

`(False, None)`

This means that the corresponding SAT instance is unsatisfiable, implying \(R_\mathrm{ref}(P_4^\mathrm{alt},P_5^\mathrm{mon})\unknown 13\). With these two executions in mind, we conclude that \(R_\mathrm{ref}(P_4^\mathrm{alt},P_5^\mathrm{mon})=13\). \(\Diamond\)

Similar to the previous two `Python` files, the `number\_finder.py` module accepts two graphs _H_<sub>1</sub> and _H_<sub>2</sub> from the graph classes of interest, satisfying \(|H_1|,|H_2|\unknown 2\), together with a string indicating which type of Ramsey number is being considered. It then computes the considered Ramsey number by solving SAT instances via the `instance\_solver.py` module for sufficiently many values of _n_. The `number\_finder.py` module can be executed using the following syntax:

`python number\_finder.py \<class\_a\> \<a\> \<class\_b\> \<b\> \<problem\_type\> \[\<starting\_n\>\]`

The first five arguments are required and have the same meaning as in the previous two modules, while the `starting\_n` argument is optional. If this argument is not provided, then the script attempts to generate and solve a SAT instance for each integer _n_ starting from the trivial lower bound max{|_H_<sub>1</sub>|,|_H_<sub>2</sub>|}, until the first unsatisfiable SAT instance is encountered or a timeout is reached. If `starting\_n` is provided and exceeds max{|_H_<sub>1</sub>|,|_H_<sub>2</sub>|}, then it is treated as a nontrivial lower bound on the considered Ramsey number, so the script attempts to generate and solve SAT instances for each integer _n_ starting from `starting\_n`. The user must guarantee that the provided `starting\_n` is a valid lower bound; otherwise, the execution will yield an incorrect result.

The main function of the `number\_finder.py` module returns an ordered pair `(exact, number)`, as follows.

**(1)** If an unsatisfiable SAT instance is encountered for the first time, this means that the corresponding _n_ is equal to the considered Ramsey number. In this case, `exact` is set to `True`, while `number` is set to the computed value of the considered Ramsey number.

**(2)** If a timeout is reached, then the corresponding _n_ is a lower bound on the considered Ramsey number, and it is not known if equality holds. In this case, `exact` is set to `False`, while `number` is set to the obtained lower bound on the considered Ramsey number.

Finally, the `grid\_explorer.py` module computes Ramsey numbers of a selected type with arguments from two provided graph classes. Although this `Python` module is based on the `bash` scripts in the `src/sat\_solving` folder from \[5\], its logic is significantly optimized to remove redundancy and improve the efficiency of extensive computation. The module can be executed using the following syntax:

`python grid\_explorer.py \<class\_a\> \<class\_b\> \<problem\_type\>`

<tbc>The three required arguments have the same meaning as in the previous modules. The `problem\_type` argument needs to be from the set {ref,dih} if at least one of the graph classes is the class of alternating paths, due to the use of Corollary 2.10.

The computation of Ramsey numbers is carried out via the `number\_finder.py` module by arranging the numbers in an infinite matrix in which the rows correspond to the orders of graphs from the first graph class, while the columns correspond to those from the second graph class. More precisely, the rows and columns correspond to the orders 3,4,5_,..._, if the graph class is not _M_<sup>nest</sup>, and 4,6,8,10_,..._, otherwise. The entries are grouped by the minimum of their row and column indices in a layer-like manner, as shown in  1. The computation proceeds layer by layer, with the last processed layer being the one whose diagonal entry is the first to yield a timeout according to the configured SAT instance generation and Kissat time limits. Within each layer, the entries are computed from the diagonal entry onward to the right and downward. In each direction, the traversal is terminated after three occurrences of a timeout or once the graph order exceeds a configurable threshold. The computation of Ramsey numbers is optimized through the use of Corollaries 2.8- 2.10. In addition, if the two graph classes corresponding to the rows and the columns are the same, then only the upper-triangular part of the infinite matrix, including the diagonal, is considered.

The `grid\_explorer.py` module also saves the computed results to a CSV file with the header `a, b, exact, number`. Here, the columns `a` and `b` specify the graph orders of the two arguments, while `number` stores the computed value. The `exact` column contains a Boolean flag indicating whether the value in the `number` column has been determined to be the exact Ramsey number or is only known to be a lower bound. The auxiliary script `table\_generator.py`, whose source code is mostly based on the `src/sat\_solving/kissat\_output\_parser.py` script from \[5\], can then be used to read all the saved CSV files and automatically generate LATEX code that displays the computed results in tables.

**Example 3.4.** Consider the following command:

`python grid\_explorer.py palt pmon ref`

This command can be used to automate the computation of Ramsey numbers of the form \(R_\mathrm{ref}(P_a^\mathrm{alt},P_b^\mathrm{mon})\) with \(a,b\ge 3\). Next, consider the following command:

`python table\_generator.py`

The execution of this command scans the saved CSV file and automatically generates the LATEX code for the corresponding table. \(\Diamond\)

The ordered and reflective Ramsey numbers of start-central stars versus start-central stars are straightforward to determine, as shown in the following proposition, which directly extends an earlier result by Balko, Cibulka, Král and Kynčl \[3, Observation 12\].

**Proposition 4.10.** _For any_ \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) _and_ \(n_1,n_2,\dots,n_k\ge 2\)_, we have_

\(R_\mathrm{ord}(S_{n_1}^\mathrm{sc},S_{n_2}^\mathrm{sc},\dots,S_{n_k}^\mathrm{sc})=R_\mathrm{ref}(S_{n_1}^\mathrm{sc},S_{n_2}^\mathrm{sc},\dots,S_{n_k}^\mathrm{sc})=\sum_{j=1}^k(n_j-2)+2.\)

_Proof._ Let \(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\dots,\Gamma_k\) be the permutation groups associated with \(S_{n_1}^\mathrm{sc},S_{n_2}^\mathrm{sc},\dots,S_{n_k}^\mathrm{sc}\), respectively, in the considered permutational Ramsey number \(R_\mathrm{type}(S_{n_1}^\mathrm{sc},S_{n_2}^\mathrm{sc},\dots,S_{n_k}^\mathrm{sc})\) with type \(\in\{\mathrm{ord},\mathrm{ref}\}\). First, we establish the upper bound. Let \(n=\sum_{j=1}^k(n_j-2)+2\), and consider a _k_-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_. Let _G<sub>j</sub>_ denote the spanning subgraph of _K<sub>n</sub>_ comprising the edges of color _j_, for \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\). By the pigeonhole principle, vertex 0 is incident to at least _n<sub>j</sub>_-1 edges of color _j_, for some \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\). Thus, there exists an increasing injective homomorphism from \(S_{n_j}^\mathrm{sc}\) to _G<sub>j</sub>_. Therefore, \(S_{n_j}^\mathrm{sc}\) is \(\Gamma_j\)-embeddable in _G<sub>j</sub>_, which implies that \(R_\mathrm{type}(S_{n_1}^\mathrm{sc},S_{n_2}^\mathrm{sc},\dots,S_{n_k}^\mathrm{sc})\le\sum_{j=1}^k(n_j-2)+2\).

Now, we establish the lower bound. Let \(n=\sum_{j=1}^k(n_j-2)+1\), and consider the _k_-edge-coloring of _K<sub>n</sub>_ in which the edge between any two distinct vertices \(u,v\in V(K_n)\) is colored with the smallest \(\ell\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\) such that \(|v-u|\le\sum_{j=1}^\ell(n_j-2)\). Let _G_<sub>1</sub>_,G_<sub>2</sub>_,...,G<sub>k</sub>_ be defined as above, and by way of contradiction, suppose that, for some \(j\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}\), \(S_{n_j}^\mathrm{sc}\) is \(\Gamma_j\)-embeddable in _G<sub>j</sub>_. Then there exists a strictly monotone injective homomorphism \(\varphi:S_{n_j}^\mathrm{sc}\rightarrow G_j\). Therefore, in _G<sub>j</sub>_, vertex \(\varphi(0)\) has at least _n<sub>j</sub>_-1 smaller neighbors or at least _n<sub>j</sub>_-1 larger neighbors, which is impossible. We conclude that \(R_\mathrm{type}(S_{n_1}^\mathrm{sc},S_{n_2}^\mathrm{sc},\dots,S_{n_k}^\mathrm{sc})\ge\sum_{j=1}^k(n_j-2)+2\).

## 5 Conclusion

We have shown how the SAT-based approach originally proposed by Poljak \[23\] for ordered Ramsey numbers and recently extended to cyclic Ramsey numbers \[4\] can be generalized to cover permutational Ramsey numbers with arbitrary associated permutation groups. Using this approach, we have computed small two-color reflective and dihedral Ramsey numbers for the following graph classes: monotone and alternating paths, monotone cycles, start-central stars, complete graphs and nested matchings. The extensive computation was automated through a pipeline of four `Python` modules based on the source code from \[5\], with significant optimizations made to improve the API and remove redundancy. We have also established several general results and formulated conjectures motivated by the computational findings.

As it turns out, although capable of obtaining lower bounds for small Ramsey numbers of both reflective and dihedral types, the SAT-based approach appears to be more efficient at providing upper bounds for reflective Ramsey numbers than for dihedral Ramsey numbers. Consequently, increasing the order of the associated permutation groups has two competing effects: while the generated SAT instances become more difficult to solve for fixed \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), the Ramsey numbers themselves tend to decrease, reducing the values of \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) that need to be considered. Our computational results further indicate that the reflective Ramsey numbers are often very close to the corresponding ordered Ramsey numbers, while the dihedral Ramsey numbers frequently coincide with the cyclic Ramsey numbers when one of the arguments is an alternating path.

We conclude with the remark that it may be worthwhile to investigate more general permutational Ramsey numbers in which the permutation groups associated with graphs are tailored to the corresponding graphs. For instance, let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), and consider the _monotone fan_ \(F_n^\mathrm{mon}\), defined as the fan graph in which 0 is adjacent to all the other vertices, while any two nonzero vertices are adjacent if and only if they are consecutive integers. Equivalently, \(F_n^\mathrm{mon}\) is the graph of order _n_ with edge set \(E(S_n^\mathrm{sc})\cup E(P_n^\mathrm{mon})\). Since 0 is a universal vertex, it is natural to associate this graph with a permutation group that fixes 0. For example, in analogy with the cyclic shift permutation, one could consider the permutation group \(\left\langle\left(012\cdots n-2n-1023\cdots n-11\right)\right\rangle\). This example illustrates one possible way in which the associated permutation groups can be chosen according to the structure of the underlying graphs. More generally, this motivates the study of permutational Ramsey numbers with arbitrary choices of associated permutation groups. Theorem 4.1 illustrates that allowing arbitrary associated permutation groups naturally leads to general results in certain cases. We believe that this could provide a fruitful direction for future research.
